More samples, the same physical wave

for sampling_rate in [3, 4, 20]:

The exact Nyquist boundary depends on phase

Return to 2 Hz; change only phase to np.pi/2. Why did the original samples almost vanish? Should we aim exactly at two samples per cycle?

Code · bold = changed / added

Run the notebook imports first. Use this block in the exercise’s work cell, or apply the bold edits to its example.

sampling_rate = 2
sample_times = np.arange(2*sampling_rate)/sampling_rate
for phase in [0, np.pi/2]:
    samples = np.sin(2*np.pi*sample_times + phase)
    plt.plot(sample_times, samples, 'o--',
             label=f'Phase = {phase:.2f} rad')
plt.xlabel('Time [s]'); plt.ylabel('Amplitude [V]')
plt.ylim(-1.2, 1.2); plt.legend(); plt.show()

Rerun the calculations after changing a parameter.

Expected answer

At phase zero, every sample lands on a zero crossing: sin(πn) ≈ 0. At π/2 the same sampling clock records +1, −1, +1, −1 V.

At exactly two samples per cycle, the recorded values depend on the starting phase. For an unknown phase, choose a sampling rate above twice the signal frequency.

Sample the shape, including its harmonics

A 20 Hz waveform uses harmonics up to nine times its fundamental. Find the highest frequency and a safe sampling condition. Why is 20 Hz alone insufficient?

Code · bold = changed / added

Run the notebook imports first. Use this block in the exercise’s work cell, or apply the bold edits to its example.

fundamental_frequency = 20
highest_harmonic = 9
highest_frequency = highest_harmonic*fundamental_frequency
boundary_rate = 2*highest_frequency
print('Highest frequency:', highest_frequency, 'Hz')
print('Use a sampling rate ABOVE', boundary_rate, 'Hz')
chosen_rate = 500  # One suitable example

Rerun the calculations after changing a parameter.

Expected answer

9 × 20 = 180 Hz; therefore choose fₛ > 360 Hz. A 500 Hz acquisition is one suitable choice for this finite harmonic sum.

The waveform’s shape includes harmonics up to 180 Hz. The sampling condition must account for those components as well as the 20 Hz fundamental.

Predict, regenerate, then measure the alias

Try sampling rates 100, 200 and 400 Hz for the fixed 153 Hz signal. Predict the peak before each run.

Code · bold = changed / added

Run the notebook imports first. Use this block in the exercise’s work cell, or apply the bold edits to its example.

frequency = 153
duration = 4
for sampling_rate in [100, 200, 400]:
    time = np.arange(duration*sampling_rate)/sampling_rate
    samples = np.sin(2*np.pi*frequency*time)
    frequencies, power_density = sp.periodogram(
        samples, fs=sampling_rate)
    peak = frequencies[np.argmax(power_density)]
    print(sampling_rate, 'samples/s ->', peak, 'Hz')
    plt.plot(frequencies, power_density,
             label=f'{sampling_rate} samples/s')
plt.xlabel('Frequency [Hz]'); plt.ylabel('PSD [V²/Hz]')
plt.legend(); plt.show()

Rerun the calculations after changing a parameter.

Expected answer

Sampling rateFolding calculationPeak
100 Hz|153 − 2×100|47 Hz
200 Hz|153 − 200|47 Hz
400 Hz|153 − 0×400|153 Hz

Use |f₀ − round(f₀/fₛ)fₛ|. Acquiring above 306 Hz retains the 153 Hz component directly.

Changing fs alone only changes the labels

Why would changing only fs in the periodogram call merely relabel existing samples?

Code · bold = changed / added

Run the notebook imports first. Use this block in the exercise’s work cell, or apply the bold edits to its example.

sampling_rate = 200
time = np.arange(4*sampling_rate)/sampling_rate
samples = np.sin(2*np.pi*153*time)
for claimed_rate in [200, 400]:
    f, density = sp.periodogram(samples, fs=claimed_rate)
    print('Claimed rate:', claimed_rate,
          'Peak label:', f[np.argmax(density)])
    plt.plot(f, density, label=f'fs label = {claimed_rate}')
plt.xlabel('Labelled frequency [Hz]')
plt.ylabel('Reported PSD [V²/Hz]'); plt.legend(); plt.show()

Notebook comparison: keep the samples fixed and change only fs in the periodogram call.

Expected answer

The same 800 samples give a peak labelled 47 Hz at fs=200 and 94 Hz at fs=400. The second label is false for this acquisition.

The samples were still recorded at 200 samples/s. Changing fs changes the frequency labels and density scale assigned to those samples. A new acquisition rate requires new measurement times and new samples.

Three physical tones, three folded peaks

Generate 433, 144 and 36 Hz at 150 samples/s. Predict and verify the peaks. What rate preserves all three physical frequencies?

Code · bold = changed / added

Run the notebook imports first. Use this block in the exercise’s work cell, or apply the bold edits to its example.

sampling_rate = 150
time = np.arange(5*sampling_rate)/sampling_rate
samples = (np.sin(2*np.pi*433*time)
           + np.sin(2*np.pi*144*time)
           + np.sin(2*np.pi*36*time))
frequencies, power_density = sp.periodogram(
    samples, fs=sampling_rate)
peaks = sp.find_peaks(power_density, height=.1)[0]
print('Observed peaks:', frequencies[peaks], 'Hz')
plt.plot(frequencies, power_density)
plt.xlabel('Frequency [Hz]'); plt.ylabel('PSD [V²/Hz]')
plt.show()

Rerun the calculations after changing a parameter.

Expected answer

433 → 17 Hz because |433−450|=17; 144 → 6 Hz because |144−150|=6; 36 → 36 Hz. The plotted peaks appear in sorted order: 6, 17, 36 Hz.

To retain every physical component directly, acquire at fₛ > 2×433 = 866 Hz, for example 1000 Hz.

Run the notebook imports first. Use this block in the exercise’s work cell, or apply the bold edits to its example.

sampling_rate = 100
time = np.arange(400)/sampling_rate
samples = (np.sin(2*np.pi*15*time)

Names: sp is the module and samples the array, avoiding the original overwritten signal name.

A working plot does not recover missing tones

What happens to 130 Hz and the zero-phase 50 Hz sine? Does a successful plot recover all three original oscillations?

Code · bold = changed / added

Run the notebook imports first. Use this block in the exercise’s work cell, or apply the bold edits to its example.

sampling_rate = 100
time = np.arange(400)/sampling_rate
boundary_samples = np.sin(2*np.pi*50*time)
alias_samples = np.sin(2*np.pi*130*time)
print('Maximum |50 Hz samples|:',
      np.max(np.abs(boundary_samples)))
print('130 Hz alias:', abs(130-round(130/100)*100))
plt.plot(time[:20], boundary_samples[:20], 'o-', label='50 Hz')
plt.plot(time[:20], alias_samples[:20], 'o-', label='130 Hz')
plt.xlabel('Time [s]'); plt.ylabel('Amplitude [V]')
plt.legend(); plt.show()

Rerun the calculations after changing a parameter.

Expected answer

The 130 Hz component aliases to 30 Hz. The zero-phase 50 Hz sine lands on its zero crossings and is numerically almost zero.

The repaired PSD shows 15 and 30 Hz. It therefore recovers only part of the original information: the 130 Hz component appears at its alias, and the 50 Hz component is missing.

Optional: phase rotates the complex coefficient

Compare phase 0, −π/2 and −π/4. Record the real part, imaginary part and magnitude. Does the 5 Hz peak move or change height?

Code · bold = changed / added

Run the notebook imports first. Use this block in the exercise’s work cell, or apply the bold edits to its example.

sampling_rate = 100
time = np.arange(200)/sampling_rate
frequency = 5
for phase in [0, -np.pi/2, -np.pi/4]:
    samples = np.cos(2*np.pi*frequency*time + phase)
    coefficients = np.fft.fft(samples)
    frequencies = np.fft.fftfreq(
        len(samples), d=1/sampling_rate)
    frequency_bin = np.argmin(abs(frequencies-frequency))
    coefficient = coefficients[frequency_bin]
    print(np.round([coefficient.real,
                    coefficient.imag, abs(coefficient)], 2))
    plt.plot(time, samples, label=f'Phase {phase:.2f}')
plt.xlim(0, .4); plt.xlabel('Time [s]')
plt.ylabel('Amplitude [V]'); plt.legend(); plt.show()

Rerun the calculations after changing a parameter.

Expected answer

PhaseRealImaginaryMagnitude
01000100
−π/20−100100
−π/470.71−70.71100

The peak stays at 5 Hz with raw magnitude 100. These 200 samples contain ten whole cycles; the physical amplitude remains 1 V.

Theory · Lecture 1, slides 11 12 19

Optional: why abs() keeps the tone visible

Why could the real part alone miss the tone? What does abs() keep, and what is lost if you discard the complex coefficients?

Code · bold = changed / added

Run the notebook imports first. Use this block in the exercise’s work cell, or apply the bold edits to its example.

sampling_rate = 100
time = np.arange(200)/sampling_rate
samples = np.cos(2*np.pi*5*time - np.pi/2)
coefficients = np.fft.fft(samples)
frequencies = np.fft.fftfreq(len(samples), d=1/sampling_rate)
positive = frequencies >= 0
plt.plot(frequencies[positive], coefficients.real[positive],
         label='Real part only')
plt.plot(frequencies[positive], np.abs(coefficients[positive]),
         label='Magnitude')
plt.xlim(0, 15); plt.xlabel('Frequency [Hz]')
plt.ylabel('Raw FFT response'); plt.legend(); plt.show()

Rerun the calculations after changing a parameter.

Expected answer

For this sine phase, the response is −100i: the real part is approximately zero. abs() combines both components as √(Re² + Im²), retaining the tone’s strength.

abs() keeps the magnitude and discards the phase. The original complex coefficients retain the starting phase needed to reconstruct the waveform.

The injected tone stays at 40 Hz. A larger standard deviation raises the typical noise background; doubling σ multiplies expected noise power by four.

At σ=0, the visible peak is the clean 40 Hz tone. As noise is added, the background rises and the tone becomes less prominent. The same draw is used at each strength.

Run notebook imports and cell 40 (L2-C15), cell 47 (L2-C18), cell 51 (L2-C20). Use this block in the exercise’s work cell, or apply the bold edits to its example.

    window='hann', nperseg=2048)

    f, noise_density = sp.welch(noise, fs=sampling_rate,
        window='hann', nperseg=2048)
    f, combined_density = sp.welch(noise+chirp_signal,
        fs=sampling_rate, window='hann', nperseg=2048)
    difference = combined_density - noise_density
    axis.plot(f, difference, label='Combined − noise')
    axis.plot(f, chirp_density, label='Chirp alone')
    axis.axhline(0, color='gray', linewidth=.7)
    axis.set(title=color)

Plot labels and formatting are included in Full code.

Expected answer

For each Fourier segment, |N+C|² − |N|² = |C|² + 2 Re(NC*). The finite-record cross term need not vanish after averaging.

The difference is therefore not exactly the chirp-only PSD. Negative values mean destructive interference in the difference, not negative physical power. Use a signed linear axis; log₁₀ is undefined for negative values.

Expected answer

Originally, 128 samples = 0.5 s, with a native spacing of 2 Hz. Padding to 8192 points made the plotted grid 0.03125 Hz, without narrowing the broad response.

Using 2048 measured samples per piece gives 8 s of information and resolves the pair, even with fewer FFT points. The figure uses density for both curves so units match. The trade-off is fewer averages and a more variable background.

Theory · Lecture 2, slides 14

Optional: fit the remaining observations, explain ambiguity

Plot the best fitted sinusoid against remaining observations. Why not assign evenly spaced times? Does Lomb–Scargle fill gaps, guarantee a unique period, or give probabilities?

Code · bold = changed / added

Run notebook imports and cell 67 (L2-C25), cell 69 (L2-C26). Use this block in the exercise’s work cell, or apply the bold edits to its example.

keep = observation_times % 1 < .25
gap_times = observation_times[keep]
gap_brightness = brightness[keep]
gap_score = sp.lombscargle(gap_times, gap_brightness,
    2*np.pi*trial_frequencies,
    normalize=True, floating_mean=True)
gap_frequency = trial_frequencies[np.argmax(gap_score)]
plot_times = np.linspace(0, 30, 1500)
fitted_curve = fit_sinusoid(
    gap_times, gap_brightness, gap_frequency, plot_times)
plt.plot(gap_times, gap_brightness, '.',
         label='Retained observations')
plt.plot(plot_times, fitted_curve, label='Best fitted sinusoid')
plt.xlim(0, 10); plt.xlabel('Time [days]')
plt.ylabel('Brightness [relative units]')
plt.legend(); plt.show()

Rerun the calculations after changing a parameter.

Expected answer

The fit uses a cosine, a sine and a constant at the actual timestamps. Replacing those times by an evenly spaced grid changes the physical problem.

Lomb–Scargle fits the available points and leaves the gaps unmeasured. Competing peaks show that several periods can fit well, so it does not guarantee a unique period. The normalized score compares the fits; it is not a probability.
